content.text: The riddle was simple enough that only the clever refused to answer it, certain a simple thing could not be true. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be.

A fox and a heron shared a meal neither could eat from the other's dish, and neither thought to change the dish. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match.

The parable does not say what became of the second river, only that the first one still speaks of it kindly. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered.

A miller ground the same grain his father ground and called it patience, though his son called it something else. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook.

The wolf hour passes quickly for those with somewhere to be, and slowly for everyone else. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful.

It is easy to mistake a closed door for a wall, the old teacher said, until someone shows you the handle. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind.

The clockmaker's apprentice asked why the wrong clock was never fixed, and was told some lessons must run on schedule. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one.

A stone thrown into either river reaches the same sea, which the valley found more comforting than either river did. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can.

The fable ends, as fables do, before anyone involved has actually learned anything, which is left to the listener. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true.

A candle argued with the dawn about which of them the room owed more to, and the room, wisely, said nothing. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it.

The ferryman's fee was a story, not a coin, and he judged each one on whether it was true or merely tidy. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been.

Two brothers split an orchard down the middle and spent the rest of their lives arguing over which half had the better light. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood.

The riddle's answer, once heard, seemed so obvious that every listener felt briefly foolish and permanently changed. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared.

A shepherd counted his flock by the shadows they threw, which worked well enough until the sun went behind a cloud. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept.

The valley kept both rivers' names on its oldest map, out of a fairness the rivers themselves never managed. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy.

What the wolf hour teaches, if it teaches anything, is that names are a convenience and not a law. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it.

The clockmaker kept one clock permanently wrong, on the theory that a man should be reminded time is not obeyed but negotiated. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

Two rivers met at the edge of the valley and argued, in their fashion, about which of them the sea would remember. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

There is an hour between dog and wolf, the old saying goes, when the light can no longer tell one from the other. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

A traveller asked the ferryman which bank was better, and the ferryman said that was a question for the far bank, not him. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved.

A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.

A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable.

The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference.

An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.
